strings.name: Marine Le Pen
strings.role: French National Assembly member and former National Rally president
strings.summary: Marine Le Pen is a French far-right politician who led the National Front and its renamed successor, National Rally. She contested three presidential elections, reaching the runoffs in 2017 and 2022. Her career spans regional councils, the European Parliament and France’s National Assembly. After relinquishing the parliamentary group presidency in 2026, she continued her presidential campaign; her conviction in the European Parliament assistants’ funding case and subsequent legal proceedings remain important to her political prospects.
strings.coverageNote: Information checked through 18 November 2026. Recent personal activity is supported by reporting on her 16 November meeting with Ukraine’s ambassador to France. Current parliamentary membership is distinguished from former group leadership, candidacy announcements from formal eligibility, and trial and appeal judgments from continuing legal review.
strings.influence.rationale: A longstanding leader of France’s nationalist political camp and repeated presidential contender, she has significantly influenced debates on immigration policy in France and Europe.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and legal education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born on 5 August 1968 in Neuilly-sur-Seine. She studied law at Paris II, obtaining a maîtrise in law in 1990, a DEA in criminal law in 1991 and the professional legal qualification in 1992. The DEA is a postgraduate diploma, not a doctorate.
strings.facts.f2.label: Professional and parliamentary roles
strings.facts.f2.value: She practised law in Paris from 1992 to 1998 before joining the National Front’s legal department. First elected to a regional council in 1998, she has represented Pas-de-Calais’s 11th constituency in the National Assembly since 2017. European, national parliamentary and party leadership roles are recorded separately.
strings.highlights.h1.title: From party leadership to national elections
strings.highlights.h1.text: She succeeded her father Jean-Marie Le Pen as National Front leader in 2011 and worked to expand its electoral reach. The party became National Rally in 2018. She placed third in the first round of the 2012 presidential election and reached the next two runoffs, without winning the presidency.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Judicial accountability and eligibility disputes
strings.highlights.h2.text: In 2026, the appeal court upheld her conviction for diverting European Parliament funds to party staff while reducing the penalties. She denies wrongdoing and seeks review by the Court of Cassation. Legal specialists disagree over whether that procedure prolongs the original electoral ban. Expert opinions are not new judgments, and a campaign announcement is not final confirmation of eligibility.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Parliamentary group succession published officially
strings.timeline.t1.text: The Assembly recorded Sébastien Chenu’s replacement of Le Pen as National Rally group president on 27 October; the notice appeared in the official gazette the next day. She retained her parliamentary seat. The group leadership change is distinct from leaving Parliament or replacing the party president.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Appeal upholds conviction and revises penalties
strings.timeline.t2.text: The sentence became three years’ imprisonment, two suspended, with the custodial portion to be served at home under electronic monitoring; a €100,000 fine; and a 45-month electoral ban, 30 months suspended. She announced her continued candidacy and sought Court of Cassation review. Enforcement and eligibility questions should not be treated as fully resolved.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Trial conviction in the parliamentary assistants case
strings.timeline.t3.text: The Paris Criminal Court imposed four years’ imprisonment, two suspended, a €100,000 fine and a five-year electoral ban with immediate enforcement. The case concerned European Parliament assistants’ funds used for party work. These trial penalties must be read alongside the changes on appeal in 2026.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Reelected in the first legislative round
strings.timeline.t4.text: She won Pas-de-Calais’s 11th constituency with 32,681 votes, or 58.04% of valid votes, in the first round. The Assembly records her new term from 1 July; the election date and start of the mandate are distinct.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Reaches a second presidential runoff
strings.timeline.t5.text: She again lost to Emmanuel Macron, receiving a final 13,288,686 votes, or 41.45% of valid votes. This presidential result is separate from her party’s seat total in the legislative election that year.
strings.timeline.t6.title: First presidential runoff
strings.timeline.t6.text: She lost to Macron with 10,638,475 votes, or 33.90% of valid votes. She entered the National Assembly that June, with her formal parliamentary term beginning on 21 June. Presidential and legislative elections are separate contests.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Elected National Front president
strings.timeline.t7.text: At the Tours congress, she defeated Bruno Gollnisch and succeeded her father as party leader. Jordan Bardella became interim president in September 2021 and was elected her successor on 5 November 2022; she is no longer the current party president.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Elected to the European Parliament
strings.timeline.t8.text: After her first election, she was reelected in 2009 and 2014. Her European Parliament service is distinct from her later membership of France’s National Assembly and does not imply a post in the European Commission.
